verdict_reason: All 30 tiles were sampled, from 3 photographers, and the pile is coherent: the identifiable architecture is all the Temple of Literature, read from its own inscriptions and fabric - the triple-arched main gate with the plaque 'Van Mieu Mon' in Chinese characters, the Dai Trung Mon gate on the axial path, the Thien Quang well with its white balustrade and longevity-roundel grille flanked by the stele galleries, the Dai Thanh hall facade, the red-lacquer shrine with bronze cranes on tortoises and gold-charactered boards, and the Thai Hoc drum. Around that core the same photographers shot the Lunar New Year fair that runs at and just outside the temple gate - stalls of red calligraphy panels bearing 'hoc', 'dang khoa', 'phuc', 'tho', peach-blossom trees, and Tet portraits against the temple's old brick walls. That is one place, and the pin sits essentially on it (about 50-100 m). It is a plausible place-centroid location, so I checked for off-topic frames and found none; a handful of portraits and stall close-ups carry no independent locational evidence, but nothing in the pile points anywhere else in the city.

photos.evidence: Close-up of a bundle of burning red incense sticks in a stone-and-metal incense trough, with a carved stone dragon's head and scaled body rising beside it and the red-lacquered lattice doors of a temple hall behind. Temple furniture consistent with the rest of the pile, but no inscription in frame, so this one is placed by context rather than by its own evidence.

The straight brick-and-stone axial path between clipped box hedges, lawns, stone lanterns and old trees, leading to a single-storey tile-roofed triple gate with white dragon ridge ornaments, with two ceremonial festival banners on poles at either side and a low balustrade beyond. That is the Dai Trung Mon gate and first courtyard of the Temple of Literature.

The square pool with a white stone balustrade and a green-painted metal grille panel decorated with circular 'tho' longevity medallions in the foreground, and across the water the two long tile-roofed stele galleries with visitors under them and a small central gate pavilion. That is the Thien Quang well courtyard of the Temple of Literature.

A paved courtyard seen along a timber verandah hung with red silk lanterns, with dark timber halls with lattice doors and tile roofs on the far side, bonsai and frangipani in stone troughs, and a raised stone walkway down the middle. Matches the Thai Hoc rear courtyard of the temple.

Interior of a red-lacquered and gilded shrine: a seated crowned figure in a canopied altar behind metal railings, flanked by gilt carved panels, tall bronze candlesticks and stone censers, with vertical red boards of gold Chinese characters on the columns and a hanging lantern. Consistent with the Dai Thanh sanctuary of the Temple of Literature.

The main gate read from its own plaque: a grey masonry gatehouse with three arched openings, an upper storey with two smaller arches, a tiled roof with dragon-and-flame ridge ornaments, and a stone tablet across the front lettered in Chinese characters as 'Van Mieu Mon'; red-painted door leaves in the arches, festival flags on poles, clipped hedges and lanterns on the approach path. That names the Temple of Literature outright.

A long open colonnade of dark timber posts under a brown pantile roof running away from the camera, interrupted by whitewashed gable pavilions carrying vertical Chinese inscriptions, standing on a tiled terrace with steps. That is one of the stele galleries housing the doctoral stelae.

The long ceremonial hall seen square-on across an empty brick-paved courtyard: an unbroken row of dark timber columns and lattice doors under a sweeping pantile roof with white dragon ridge scrolls, red lanterns hung between the bays and bonsai in stone pots along the front. That is the Bai Duong / Dai Thanh hall of the Temple of Literature.

Inside the ceremonial hall: two large bronze cranes standing on tortoises beside a gilded altar, a row of red-lacquered columns with vertical gold-charactered boards hanging on them, carved and gilded panels above, and a horizontal Chinese-inscribed board over the bay. The crane-on-tortoise pair and gilded altar match the Temple of Literature's Dai Thanh interior.

A young man reaching up to touch the head of a very large drum with a studded rim, mounted in a red timber frame under a roof, with bare peach branches in the foreground and greenery and crowds behind. A ceremonial drum of that size in a red pavilion matches the Thai Hoc drum tower at the Temple of Literature, where the same photographer's other frames are set.

Portrait of a young man in a leather jacket against a red brick wall laid in an old bond with wide mortar joints, shot along the wall so it recedes out of focus. The wall type matches the temple's brick enclosure walls used as a backdrop by this photographer's other Tet portraits, but the frame carries no independent locational evidence.

A young man standing in front of a flowering peach tree with a crowd of visitors in winter coats behind and a stone step and railing at the left. A Lunar New Year crowd around peach blossom; peach sellers and blossom displays cluster at the temple during Tet, and the rest of this photographer's sequence is there, but nothing in the frame itself names the spot.

Another young man posed in front of a tall flowering peach tree with festival crowds and a red-clad stall behind. Same Tet blossom display as 6764399025 and 6764413681; placed by context, not by its own detail.

A man photographed through a pierced opening in an old brick wall, the wall filling the frame out of focus with the figure sharp in the gap. Pierced brick openings in weathered walls of this kind are part of the temple's enclosure that this photographer works around all through the set; the frame alone gives only the wall.

A couple posed outdoors with a blurred street behind them - low pastel buildings, a fan palm, a blue hoarding and pavement trees - so this one is on the road outside rather than in a courtyard. Consistent with Van Mieu street at the temple's gate, where the rest of the sequence is, but no street plate or shopfront is legible.

A couple standing in front of tall dark red-brown timber lattice doors and columns of a traditional hall, with the paving of a courtyard at their feet. The joinery matches the temple halls in this pile's architectural frames, but there is no inscription in shot.

Four people posed in a dense Lunar New Year crowd on brick paving, with an old brick wall, a tile-roofed timber structure and a horizontal Chinese-charactered board visible behind them and bare peach branches across the foreground. The paving, wall and inscribed board place this inside the temple courtyards during the Tet crowds.

Tight portrait of a man holding a small child in a woolly hat, with an out-of-focus festival crowd and a stone edge behind. No architecture is resolvable; placed only by belonging to the same Tet sequence.

A young woman posing beside a potted flowering peach tree in a red ceramic pot, under a red silk lantern hung from a tiled eave, with a New Year crowd behind. The tiled eave with hanging red lantern matches the temple courtyards dressed for Tet in this pile's other frames.

Portrait of a young man leaning against dark timber joinery beside an old brick reveal, greenery out of focus behind. Same backdrop family as the other portraits in this sequence; no independent locational detail.

Red and cream calligraphy scrolls painted with large Chinese characters hung in a row from the eaves of an old timber building with a brown pantile roof and whitewashed piers, with more stalls receding behind. This is the Tet calligraphy fair that sets up at and immediately outside the Temple of Literature, whose galleries this building matches.

A young woman in a black jacket standing beside a tall stand hung with dense bunches of red-tasselled charms and small brass bells, with festival crowds behind. A Tet charm stall of the kind that lines the temple's calligraphy fair; no sign or building in frame.

Close-up of rows of hanging good-luck charms - red silk tassels below white round medallions and fans printed with characters - strung on a rail at a fair stall. The goods place it at a Tet fair rather than at any particular street; assigned to the temple fair by context with the rest of this photographer's set.

A woman holding a slip of paper and a brush-like stick beside a stall wall covered in packets and red hangings, with another customer beside her. A calligraphy or charm stall at the Tet fair; nothing in frame is location-specific.

Rows of hanging red charms and amulets in the foreground with fair-goers browsing between the stalls behind, one stall showing a red vertical banner. Same fair as this photographer's other frames; no legible text.

Rows of red and cream calligraphy panels hung under a carved timber eave, each painted with a single large Chinese character - among them 'hoc' (study), 'hieu' (filial piety), 'tam', 'nhan', 'tho', 'phuc', 'duc', 'dat' and the pair 'dang khoa' (passing the examination). Examination-success calligraphy sold under a temple eave is the Tet fair at the Temple of Literature, the shrine of the imperial examinations.
A man in a pale jacket at a stall thickly hung with red charm bundles, amulets and knotted tassels, other shoppers' hands in the foreground. Same Tet charm fair; no building or sign visible.

A woman in a white floral ao dai posed with her hand on a weathered old brick wall, a dark timber door beside her, the wall receding out of focus along the frame. The lime-mortared old brickwork and timber door match the temple's enclosure walls, which this photographer uses as the backdrop for a short portrait series.
Second frame of the same ao dai portrait series against the same weathered brick wall with mortar-smeared courses, the subject turned towards the camera. Placed by continuity with 8638886135.

Third frame of the ao dai series, shot along the same old brick wall so it recedes steeply out of focus, the subject standing against it in profile. Same wall and same session as 8638886135 and 8639988142.
